rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān denotes unqualified, boundless mercy prior to creation; it is also rendered “the Infinitely Good” or “the Loving.”
rows.anchor: al-Raḥmān, which is considered to denote that aspect of mercy and compassion that is unqualified, boundless, and prior to the created order.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān is uniquely divine because existence is made manifest through this Name as a universal mercy that cannot be attributed to another.
rows.anchor: one of the Divine Names that can only apply to God, for it is one of the Names by which existence itself is made manifest

rows.speaker: Sufis
rows.claim: Many Sufis say that all creation is brought forth through the Breath of the Compassionate.
rows.anchor: many Sufis say that all of creation is brought forth through “the Breath of the Compassionate.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥīm denotes more particular Divine mercy and can describe humans; al-Raḥmān relates to the Essence, while al-Raḥīm refers to mercy extended through God's acts.
rows.anchor: a more particular form of Divine Mercy and by which human beings may also be described.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān relates more directly to the Divine Essence, while al-Raḥīm refers to God's mercy extended in all acts.
rows.anchor: al-Raḥmān relates more directly to the Divine Essence, while al-Raḥīm can be seen as referring to the extension of God’s Mercy in all acts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Compassionate is said to assume God's Throne.
rows.anchor: the Compassionate who is said to assume the Throne of God in 20:5 (cf. 25:59).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb's placement after al-Raḥmān makes teaching revelation intrinsic to God's compassion; revelation is a blessing sustaining creation.
rows.anchor: That the verb taught comes directly after the Divine Name al-Raḥmān indicates that teaching revelation is intrinsic to God’s compassionate nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Teaching is an essential divine function toward humanity: God teaches Adam and all humans, created for knowledge, before giving commands, laws, and judgment.
rows.anchor: human beings are created for knowledge and God teaches Adam and thus all of humanity (2:31) before commanding, providing laws, and judging.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators read the verse as an answer to disbelievers who claimed a human taught the Prophet and the Quran.
rows.anchor: According to some commentators, this verse is a direct response to the disbelievers who said

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others see an allusion to God's making the Quran easy to learn, echoed by the preceding sūrah's refrain.
rows.anchor: Others understand it as an allusion to the manner in which God has made the Quran easy to learn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse may instead begin a new thought: God taught the Quran.
rows.anchor: This verse could also be understood as the beginning of a new thought

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “Possessed of Majesty and Bounty” closes the discussion of heavenly blessings, echoing its role at 55:27 for earthly blessings.
rows.anchor: here it marks the end of the discussion of heavenly blessings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the phrase modifies “thy Lord,” as it modified “the Face of thy Lord” at 55:27.
rows.anchor: Here it modifies thy Lord, just as it modified the Face of thy Lord in v. 27.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A canonical reading construes “Possessed of Majesty and Bounty” as modifying “Name,” reading dhū rather than dhī.
rows.anchor: According to another canonical reading, Possessed of Majesty and Bounty could here be read as modifying the Name (i.e., dhū, rather than dhī; Q, Z).

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet advised followers to persist in invoking “O Possessor of Majesty and Bounty.”
rows.anchor: It is said that the Prophet advised his followers, “Persist [in invoking] ‘O Possessor of Majesty and Bounty’” (IK).

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: An account attributed to ʿĀʾishah says the Prophet often prayed after prayers, “O God, Thou art Peace, and peace comes from Thee. Blessed art Thou, Possessed of Majesty and Bounty.”
rows.anchor: account attributed toʿĀʾishah that after prayers the Prophet would often sit and say

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is one of many verses enjoining human beings to glorify God.
rows.anchor: This is one of many verses in which human beings are enjoined to glorify God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command can also mean glorifying by God's Name, thus commanding invocation of the Name.
rows.anchor: It can also mean, “Glorify by the Name of thy Lord,” thus indicating a command to invoke the Name of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasbīḥ means declaring something transcendent beyond everything else.
rows.anchor: The term for “glorification,”tasbīḥ, indicates declaring something transcendent beyond all else.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though God is responsible for the matters in 56:58–73, He transcends them: He performs many other tasks and their perceived deficiencies cannot be attributed to Him.
rows.anchor: although God is responsible for all of the things mentioned in vv. 58–73, He is completely beyond them

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Bḍ allows “the Magnificent” to modify either “Name” or “Lord.”
rows.anchor: The Magnificent can be taken to modify either Name or Lord (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Aj also reads the verse as a command to glorify God, whose Glory exceeds anything anyone can say of it.
rows.anchor: This verse can also be seen as a command to glorify God, since God’s Glory is beyond what anyone else can say of it (Aj).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refers to the soul reaching the throat at death, as 75:26–28 describes its reaching the collarbones and the parting.
rows.anchor: It is a reference to the soul when it reaches the throat at the moment of death, as in 75:26–28

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is always nearer to people than they are to themselves and has power over them despite their contrary illusions, as 50:16 says.
rows.anchor: God is nearer to human beings at all times than they are to themselves, and He has power over them at every moment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At death, 6:61–62 describes God sending guardians, whose messengers take the dying; people then return to their true Master, to whom judgment belongs.
rows.anchor: The manner in which God exercises this power at the moment of death is most clearly expressed in 6:61–62

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If people owe God their lives and are not independently responsible for them, they cannot control the moment of death when the soul returns whence it came.
rows.anchor: If you do not owe your life to God and are yourself responsible for it, why do you not control the moment of death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the challenge asks why people cannot return the soul to the body after it has reached the throat.
rows.anchor: Why are you unable to return the soul to the body after it has reached the throat?” (Aj, IK, Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayr madīnīn, translated “unconstrained,” can also mean “not indebted.”
rows.anchor: Unconstrained translates ghayr madīnīn, which could also mean “if you are not indebted,”indicating

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If people own their souls and owe no debt to God, they should control where the soul came from and where it goes.
rows.anchor: you should be able to control whence it came and whither it will go.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage is called among the “Jewels of the Quran” and is often recited in obligatory and supererogatory prayers.
rows.anchor: This passage is considered to be among the “Jewels of the Quran”and is often recited in both obligatory and supererogatory prayers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage gives the Quran's most extensive list of Divine Names: seventeen, or eighteen if the opening pronoun huwa is counted.
rows.anchor: It provides the most extensive list of Divine Names in the Quran, seventeen in all—or eighteen, if one includes the pronoun He

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many regard the opening pronoun huwa as a Divine Name pertaining to the Divine Essence.
rows.anchor: which many consider a Divine Name pertaining to the Divine Essence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sayings extol recitation of the sūrah's final three verses, sometimes including 59:21.
rows.anchor: Many sayings extol the recitation of this sūrah, especially these last three verses (sometimes including v. 21 as well).

rows.speaker: Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ
rows.claim: Fuḍayl says that one who reads 59:21–24 in the morning and dies that day, or reads it in the evening and dies that night, is marked among those who witness God.
rows.anchor: According to one saying attributed to the early Ḥadīth specialist Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ (d. 187/803),

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage begins with the Islamic testimony of faith, explained at 2:255.
rows.anchor: with which this passage begins, see 2:255c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Name Allāh is all-comprehensive because it comprises the particular qualities conveyed by the other Divine Names.
rows.anchor: The Name Allāh—“God”—is referred to as the all-comprehensive Name

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allāh is the most specific Divine Name because it cannot describe any being other than God, unlike names such as Merciful or Clement.
rows.anchor: It is also the most specific of the Names, since it cannot be used to describe any being other than God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Knower of the Unseen and the seen” means God knows all that is hidden and manifest on every level of reality, in this world and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: God knows all that is hidden and all that is manifest on all levels of reality, in both this world and the Hereafter

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Aj offers an alternative: God knows things before they appear in external existence as unseen, and afterward as seen.
rows.anchor: It can also mean that God knows all things before they become manifest in external existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meanings of “the Compassionate, the Merciful” are discussed at 1:3.
rows.anchor: Regarding the Compassionate, the Merciful, see 1:3c.

rows.speaker: Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazzālī
rows.claim: Al-Ghazzālī sees the first five Names as progressing from those closer to the Divine Essence to those closer to Divine Action.
rows.anchor: According to Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazzālī in his Commentary on the Most Beautiful Names of God, there is a progression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Sovereign needs no other being in His Essence or Attributes, while all other things need Him.
rows.anchor: The Sovereign is the One Who in both His Essence and His Attributes has no need of any other being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Holy wholly transcends any quality humans might attribute to Him, so His Perfection exceeds human conception.
rows.anchor: The Holy is the One Who transcends utterly any quality that one might attribute to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Peace means flawless, beyond imperfection, and untouched by evil or inner contradiction.
rows.anchor: Peace translates ṣalām, which indicates being flawless, beyond all imperfections, and untarnished by any evil or inner contradiction.

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: When some Companions prayed “Peace upon God,” the Prophet corrected them, teaching that God Himself is Peace.
rows.anchor: some Companions used to pray “Peace upon God,” until the Prophet corrected them, indicating that God was Himself Peace.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Muʾmin, also used for human “believers,” means that God provides all safety and security.
rows.anchor: The Faithful translates al-Muʾmin, the same word that is rendered “believer” when used to describe human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Protector watches over creation and tends continually to creatures' actions and provision.
rows.anchor: The Protector is the One Who watches over His creation, tending to their actions and their provision at every moment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Mighty is eminent, needed by others, and difficult to access.
rows.anchor: The Mighty indicates the One Who is eminent, of Whom others have need and to Whom access is difficult.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Compeller's Will prevails over every other will; nothing escapes His grasp, and nothing can grasp Him.
rows.anchor: The Compeller is the One Whose Will prevails over the will of all others, the One Whose grasp nothing escapes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Proud is majestic to the exclusion of all else; nothing is worthy of being considered in relation to Him.
rows.anchor: The Proud is the One Who is majestic to the exclusion of all else

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creator, Maker, and Fashioner describe stages of creation: measuring before existence, bringing into being, then giving form and characteristics.
rows.anchor: The Creator indicates the Quality of God through which He measures things out before they come into existence in this world; the Maker

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Alternatively, the three Names refer to stages through which creatures, especially humans, develop in the womb.
rows.anchor: these three Divine Names can be seen as referring more specifically to the three stages through which creatures, in particular human beings, develop in the womb (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “unto Him belong the Most Beautiful Names” is linked with 7:180, 17:110, and 20:8.
rows.anchor: Regarding unto Him belong the Most Beautiful Names (cf. 7:180; 17:110; 20:8)

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A famous ḥadīth says God has ninety-nine Names and whoever enumerates them will enter the Garden.
rows.anchor: a famous ḥadīth states, “God has ninety-nine Names—one hundred minus one—and whosoever enumerates them will enter the Garden” (IK)

rows.speaker: many scholars
rows.claim: Many scholars hold that God has more than ninety-nine Names, many unrevealed to humans.
rows.anchor: though many scholars maintain that God has more than ninety-nine Names, many of which are not revealed to human beings.

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to invoke God by every Name He has used for Himself, revealed in Scripture, taught to creation, or kept in unseen knowledge.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have called upon God saying, “I implore Thee by every Name that is Thine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mumtahanah is a Madinan sūrah, most likely revealed after 6/628.
rows.anchor: A Madinan sūrah, al-Mumtaḥanah was most likely revealed sometime after the year 6/628.

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some date the first verse to the Muslim conquest of Makkah in 8/630.
rows.anchor: Some maintain that the first verse was revealed on the day Makkah was conquered by the Muslim army in 8/630.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title comes from the command to examine the women in 60:10; as translated, it refers to Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah, about whom several verses were reportedly revealed.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from the injunction to examine them in v. 10.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is also called al-Imtiḥān, “The Examining” or “The Examiner,” describing its exposure of human faults, a quality shared by the Quran.
rows.anchor: It is also known as al-Imtiḥān, “The Examining” (Āl) or“The Examiner,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another title, al-Mawaddah (“Affection”), likely comes from 60:1 and 60:7 and reflects the sūrah's teaching on where believers' affections should lie.
rows.anchor: Some have also named this sūrah al-Mawaddah, “Affection” (Āl), most likely after the phrases you offer them affection (v. 1) and God will forge affection (v. 7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 60:1–3 prohibit affection for or alliances with an enemy party.
rows.anchor: That there should be no affection for or alliances with an enemy party is made clear in vv. 1–3.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham and his followers in 60:4–6 provide an example to follow in disavowing enemy parties.
rows.anchor: The case of Abraham and his followers is then cited as an example to be followed (vv. 4–6)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 60:7–9 offer hope for improved relations with enemies and permit good relations with those who do not oppose Muslims.
rows.anchor: provides hope that better relations can be established with enemy parties and allows for good relations with those who do not oppose the Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section addresses women emigrating from Makkah to Madinah and rules for women married to idolaters who embrace Islam.
rows.anchor: The last section (vv. 10–12) addresses the complex situation brought about by the emigration of women from Makkah to Madinah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marriages between believers and disbelievers were thereafter invalid and were to be dissolved as equitably as possible.
rows.anchor: Marriages between believers and disbelievers were henceforth considered invalid, but were to be dissolved in as equitable a manner as possible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse was reportedly revealed about poor Muslims who informed Jews of Muslim activities in exchange for provisions.
rows.anchor: This verse was reportedly revealed regarding some poor Muslims who would inform the Jews of the activities of the Muslims in exchange for provisions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes with an injunction like its opening: do not take God's enemies as friends.
rows.anchor: the sūrah ends with an injunction similar to the one with which it began—to not take God’s enemies as friends

rows.speaker: Jews of Madinah
rows.claim: One interpretation identifies those who despair of the Hereafter as Jews of Madinah despairing because they denied Muhammad's prophethood.
rows.anchor: They have despaired of the Hereafter refers to the Jews of Madinah, who would be in despair for denying the prophethood of Muhammad

rows.speaker: hypocrites
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies them as hypocrites who would despair because they conspired against the Prophet.
rows.anchor: or to the hypocrites, who would despair for conspiring against the Prophet (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase can also refer generally to those who despair of the Hereafter because they preferred and worked only for worldly life.
rows.anchor: It can also be seen as a reference to all those who despair of the Hereafter because they preferred and thus worked only for this world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers in the comparison specifically mean the pagan Makkans, and the two groups will be punished in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: That they despair as do the disbelievers, here referring specifically to the idolatrous Makkans, indicates that both will be punished in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Despair of the inhabitants of graves” may mean disbelievers do not expect to see deceased relations because they reject the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: the manner in which the disbelievers despair of seeing their deceased relations because they have no concept of a Hereafter (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase means disbelievers believe no good will come to those who die as disbelievers.
rows.anchor: or to the belief that no good will come to those who die as disbelievers (Q).
